chief_complaint: painless soft mobile subcutaneous mass on back
hpi_details: A 50-year-old woman reports a painless, soft, freely mobile subcutaneous mass on her back that has enlarged slowly without skin change or neurologic symptoms.
ideas: She thinks it might be a harmless fatty buildup or a clogged sweat gland caused by pressure from her clothing.
concerns: She is worried that the soft mass might turn out to be a hidden cancerous tumor like the one her sister had.
expectations: She hopes to get an ultrasound today to verify that the mass is entirely benign.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Trunk Lipoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Trunk Lipoma: Reassure, surgical excision if large or causing cosmetic concern, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Trunk Lipoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Failing to image or refer a rapidly enlarging, deep, fixed, large, or painful mass.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: When did you first notice this lump, and how long has it been there?
Has it grown in size, and if so how quickly?
Is the lump painful, and does it move freely under your skin?
Has the skin over the lump changed color or become fixed to it?

must_ask.objective: Prior similar lumps or family history
must_ask.say: Have you had similar lumps before, or does anyone in your family get them?

history.answer: I noticed a soft lump on my upper back a while ago, and I came in today to have it checked out.
I first noticed it about a year ago while taking a shower.
It is located on my upper back, just to the right of my spine.
It has grown very slowly over the past year, maybe just a little bit larger than when I first discovered it.
It is about the size of a golf ball, around three or four centimeters across, and it is the only lump I have found.
It feels soft and squishy, and it slides around easily under the skin when I press on it.
No, it does not hurt at all, even when I press firmly on it or lean against the back of a chair.
No, the skin looks completely normal with no discoloration, dark spots, or unusual moles.
No, it has never bled, developed a scab, or broken open.
No, there is no redness, the skin does not feel hot, and nothing has ever leaked out of it.
No, there is no central dark dot or hole, and I have never seen any cheesy or foul-smelling material come out.
No, it stays the same size all the time and does not swell up with activity or movement.
No, I have never had an injury, cut, surgery, acne, or piercing in that area.
No, I have never tried to squeeze, pop, or puncture it, and I haven't received any treatment for it.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweats.
No, my weight has been completely stable, and I haven't had any night sweats or unexplained fatigue.
No, I haven't felt any swollen glands or other lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
No, I don't have any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my back or arms.
No, my back is not exposed to the sun, and I have never had severe blistering sunburns.
Neither I nor anyone in my family has ever been diagnosed with skin cancer, melanoma, or any other tumors.
No one in my family has had multiple soft fatty lumps or similar skin growths that I know of.
I don't have any chronic medical problems like diabetes, hypertension, or immune disorders.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe one glass of wine once or twice a month.
I work as an administrative office clerk and live with my husband and daughter.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, my periods are regular, and there is no possibility that I am pregnant.
I thought it was probably just a harmless little ball of fat or a clogged gland from my clothes rubbing against it.
My sister had a malignant tumor that started as an innocent lump, so I'm really anxious that this is cancer.
I'm hoping you can do a quick scan or ultrasound today just to confirm that it's not dangerous.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.6°C, SpO2 99% on room air.
Comfortable, well-nourished woman in no acute distress.
On the right upper back, a 3.5 x 3.0 cm soft, lobulated, freely mobile subcutaneous mass without overlying erythema, warmth, punctum, or transillumination; remainder of skin examination is clear.
Mass is located within the subcutaneous tissue without fixation to underlying deep fascia or thoracic musculature, and non-tender to deep palpation.
No palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy bilaterally.
No palpable axillary lymphadenopathy bilaterally; normal breast tissue.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation throughout the back and upper extremities without focal neurologic deficits.
Normal spinal alignment with no midline vertebral or paraspinal tenderness, and full range of motion.
